title: Tronox upgraded to Neutral at J.P. Morgan as shares near all-time lows - TradingView
content: Tronox TROX jumped 7.2% in Monday's trading as J.P. Morgan upgraded the titanium dioxide pigment manufacturer to Neutral from Underweight, even as demand for TiO2 is constrained by negative paint industry volumes in the U.S. and Europe, and the industry is oversupplied. However, J.P. Morgan analyst Jeffrey Zekauskas said he withdrew his price target for Tronox TROX given uncertain and negative business conditions in the context of the quality of the company’s long-term business franchise in a lower interest rate and raw materials environment. Demand conditions are difficult and costs are rising, and 2027 may provide an environment in which prices and volumes in titanium dioxide are at best flat, the analyst said, forecasting Tronox's TROX free cash flow likely will be negative by ~$40M in 2026 excluding dividends and by $72M including dividends, adding that cash flows were assisted in 2026 by a ~$70M working capital benefit, which is not expected to recur in 2027. China's TiO2 export shipments to India are higher by 46% YTD, and China shipments to Europe are nearly 25% higher despite high tariffs; however, India has newly placed tariffs on Chinese product, which Zekauskas said should provide Tronox TROX and Chemours CC with a total volume opportunity of ~200K tons in 2027. title: JPMorgan Just Removed Alphabet From Its Analyst Focus List - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor) This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. JPMorgan (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction) removed Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) from its Analyst Focus List but kept its Overweight rating on the stock. The firm pointed to slower AI search monetization and heavy AI infrastructure spending. JPMorgan lowered its near-term confidence in Alphabet stock without giving up its longer-term bullish view. JPMorgan finds stronger near-term momentum at Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) than at Alphabet. The third-quarter results show where the pressure is. Search revenue grew 12% to $63.3 billion, even though query growth was the highest in five years. On the earnings call, JPMorgan’s Douglas Anmuth asked about that gap. Alphabet’s chief business officer said that strong growth in AI Mode queries “had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.” Is Now The Time To Buy For Alphabet, Microsoft or Nvidia? Spending is the other concern. Capex reached $51.4 billion in the quarter, and free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. Meetings begin this week and centre on how firms would build scheme and to what timetable The Docklands site where JP Morgan plans to build its new Fosters-designed headquarters Three contractors are set to make presentations to JP Morgan Chase about how they would build its new Foster + Partners-designed headquarters building in Canary Wharf. Building Design’s sister title Building understands a series of so-called ‘beauty parade’ meetings are being held from this week with teams from Multiplex, Mace Construct and Bovis outlining how they would build the tower, the supply chain they would use and project timetables. How the job would be procured is also set to be discussed. Sir Robert McAlpine is also understood to have been asked to go along with firms told to outline how they would build a building which will be one of the biggest construction jobs in the capital in the coming years. It is understood firms have not been asked to work up a price for the tower, which is in the early stages of the planning process. Foster + Partners recently submitted a related planning application to build a 180m-long park over an existing road next to the planned site of the headquarters scheme. The new park is intended to improve the public realm around the site and strengthen connectionsn to the centre of Canary Wharf. Plans to build a 180m-long park over an existing road were recently submitted by Foster + Partners. The scheme is intended to improve the public realm around the future JP Morgan headquarters. The meetings come as JP Morgan, which declined to comment, has been building its project team for the job with last month the bank appointing Real PM co-founder Jeremy Ruff as real estate managing director with a brief to work on the tower. Others who have been recruited in recent months include Alinea co-founder Steve Watts, British Land’s former head of development delivery Alan Bunting while Building understands the bank is due to make another senior appointment imminently. No details of how tall the tower will be or what it will look like have been released but it is understood Fosters had originally come up with three options and what is known is that it will run across three million sq ft and be home to 12,000 employees while flight path regulations in the area mean it cannot be more than 265m high. The cost of the JP Morgan scheme has been put at £10bn and will be built on the Riverside South plot that was due to be developed by the bank nearly 20 years ago before being put on hold because of the financial crash. JP Morgan’s main base at Canary Wharf is 25 Bank Street. But the firm has outgrown the space and plans to fit 12,000 staff in at its planned HQ at Riverside South The job will be one of several huge schemes coming up in London with others on the blocks including 99 Bishopsgate, a 54-storey tower designed by RSHP and due to be built by Multiplex with packages for the cladding and steelwork alone both believed to be in excess of £100m. Other jobs include 1 Undershaft, now called One London, and Exchequer Court – designed by Wilkinson Eyre – both of which are 70 storeys tall. That scheme is being spearheaded by George Iacobescu, Canary Wharf’s former chairman and chief executive, who is also advising JP Morgan on its Riverside South job. Multiplex has been providing pre-construction advice on Exchequer Court with the job due in for planning before Christmas while Keltbray is carrying out demolition work at the site of One London which has been designed by Eric Parry. title: JPMorgan Stock Slides on Epstein Probe Fears: Bitcoin Has No CEO to Drag Into the Scandal - CryptoPotato
content: Alongside the rest of the market, shares of JPMorgan Chase tanked at the end of the previous week, but there’s more to the story. JPM’s decline also came after reports emerged that Senate Democrats are preparing a fresh investigation into the banking behemoth’s relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Although there’s no real connection with Bitcoin, we decided to still cover this and highlight the awkwardness, as JPM’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, has spent years bashing the crypto industry. CNBC reported after the Blue-nami in the US midterms that Democratic staff on the Senate Finance Committee plan to examine how senior JPM executives handled Epstein as they take control of Congress early next year. Mary Erdoes, CEO of the bank’s Asset & Wealth Management Division, is expected to be among the high-profile names in the investigations. “The US government had damning information ​about Epstein’s crimes that it failed to share ​with us or other banks. We regret any association we had with ‌him, ⁠but we did not help him commit his crimes,” commented a spokesperson from the bank. The market reaction was immediate as JPM shares tanked by over 4% to under $340 on Thursday. The sell-off essentially erased the stock’s post-midterm rally. Although the bank continues to deny any wrongdoing, it previously agreed to pay $365 million in settlements related to Epstein. We admit there’s no official confirmation that JPM has done anything wrong, and we don’t expect it to come to light if it did, because it’s one of the world’s largest banks. And we know how banks are treated in almost any situation (recall the 2008 banking crisis and the subsequent lack of any real consequences). Nevertheless, the irony is still worth pointing out. JPM’s long-serving CEO, Jamie Dimon, has been bashing BTC for years. He has called it a “fraud,” “worthless,” a “pet rock,” and a “decentralized Ponzi scheme.” All bad and, in some cases, illegal names. He also advised investors to stay away from crypto and told lawmakers that if he were running the US government, he would “close it down.” The hypocrisy is glaring when we look at what the bank has done lately. It now lets institutional clients use BTC and ETH as collateral; it supports crypto-related services; it participated in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF infrastructure; and it recently projected that bitcoin could outperform US large-cap stocks and gold over the next 10-15 years. But there’s another contrast. Bitcoin has no CEO, board of directors, wealth-management division, or customer relationship with Jeffrey Epstein – or anyone else, for that matter. The protocol itself cannot make a questionable client decision, hide internal correspondence, or become subject to congressional scrutiny over corporate conduct. People or companies using BTC can still appear in investigations and criminal records, but reputational and governance risks belong to institutions and individuals, not the decentralized Bitcoin network itself. title: JPMorgan vs. Bank of America: Which Dividend Stock Is Better for Retirement? - AOL.com
content: JPMorgan beats Bank of America as the retirement dividend pick, with a thicker capital cushion and faster payout growth outweighing a slightly lower starting yield. JPMorgan lifted its quarterly dividend about 57% since early 2024, while Bank of America managed roughly 33%. Bank of America trades at a steep discount and yields about 3% versus JPMorgan's 2%, suiting investors with a decade-plus horizon. Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor) JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) or Bank of America (NYSE:BAC): which bank dividend looks stronger for someone building a retirement portfolio right now? Third-quarter earnings made the choice clearer. Bank of America posted adjusted EPS of $1.08, missing the $1.10 estimate, after a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge. JPMorgan reported EPS of $5.57 and a 20% return on tangible common equity. In September, it had already raised its quarterly dividend to $1.65 from $1.50. Both banks make money in the same two ways. The first is net interest income, the gap between what they earn on loans and what they pay on deposits. The second is fees from trading, dealmaking, and wealth management. title: JP Morgan Athlete Center of Excellence: athletes need a financial playbook now more than ever - Fortune
content:
Adam Frank is head of wealth planning and advice at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management. He and his team are responsible for wealth planning, thought leadership and strategic planning for individual clients, and he oversees the firm’s Athlete Center of Excellence. J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence and the JPMorganChase Athlete Council are both named in this piece. For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth. That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it. Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they’re still in school. At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes. There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them. Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made. The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust? These aren’t professional athlete questions. They’re life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before. One thing I’ve learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence is that they’re eager for this guidance. I’ve spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I’ve seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant. Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts. Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions. I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don’t have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future. That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today’s athletes aren’t just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age. The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it. The answer isn’t limiting opportunity for athletes. It’s building a stronger foundation of education and support around it. First, we need to start earlier. Financial fundamentals should be introduced in high school, before athletes encounter significant earnings. By the time money arrives, the framework for managing it should already be in place. Second, financial education cannot be a one-time conversation. Athletes’ needs evolve as they move from high school to college, turn professional and transition out of sports. The guidance they receive should evolve alongside them. One of the reasons the JPMorganChase Athlete Council was created was to hear directly from athletes. This way, we can better understand the financial questions they’re facing and develop resources that reflect their real-world experiences, not our assumptions. Athletic careers are unlike almost any other profession. Most people earn income over several decades. Athletes often earn a huge portion of their career income over a much shorter period of time. Opportunities can arrive unexpectedly, and they can disappear just as quickly. If we want athletes to thrive not only during their playing careers but throughout the rest of their lives, we need to start with financial education long before the first major paycheck arrives.
